confounds: The label distribution is highly imbalanced: 618 diagnosed users versus 5,463 controls; all reported comparisons are user-level rather than raw post shares.

Diagnosed users were more active on average (about 623 versus 527 retained posts/user), so full-timeline any-match rates are activity-sensitive; first-50/first-100 analyses and matched-posts-per-user were used as checks.
Quotation, lyrics, retweets, news, advocacy, third-person discussion, jokes, and idiomatic hyperbole cannot be perfectly separated from personal experience using text-only heuristics.
Source order supports persistence checks across timeline segments but does not guarantee temporal chronology or clinical duration.
Differences may reflect self-disclosure, healthcare contact, demographics, fandom or community composition, posting style, collection artifacts, or annotation practices rather than depression itself.
Portuguese slang, spelling variation, and polysemy create both false positives and missed symptom expressions.

negative_results: Perceived-failure language did not generalize: overall prevalence was 27.2% diagnosed versus 25.7% control; first-100-post differences by folds 1–4 were +0.9, +1.9, −2.4, and +2.2 percentage points.
Guilt was mixed after exposure control: first-100 differences were −1.9, +2.6, −2.9, and −1.8 percentage points.
Punishment/blame language was not diagnosed-enriched: full-timeline prevalence was 62.0% diagnosed versus 62.3% control, and controls were higher in the first 100 posts in all folds.

Sleep, energy/fatigue, irritability, and concentration were not fold-stable after exposure control. Sleep first-100 differences were −1.0, +6.0, +3.6, and +7.0 points; energy was +0.8, +0.3, −0.9, and +5.4.
Broad worthlessness terms were higher overall, but self-framed early evidence was mixed; insults often targeted other people, objects, fandoms, or situations.
No evidence supported clinically interpretable libido loss; only general sexual-topic vocabulary was elevated.
Generic interest, indecision, food, sleep, and fatigue words were frequent in both groups and are poor standalone BDI proxies.
